title: Law of Sines Checkpoint
description: Show that you can solve ASA, AAS, and SSA oblique triangle problems using the Law of Sines.

questions.question: In △ABC, side a is opposite which angle?
questions.explanation: By standard notation, lowercase side a is opposite uppercase angle A.

questions.question: In △ABC, ∠A = 36°, ∠B = 79°, and b = 18. Which expression finds a?
questions.explanation: Use a/sin 36° = 18/sin 79°, so a = 18 sin 36° / sin 79°.

questions.question: In △ABC, ∠A = 36°, ∠B = 79°, and b = 18. What is a to the nearest tenth?
In △ABC, ∠A = 46°, ∠C = 80°, and c = 18. What is a to the nearest tenth?
In △ABC, ∠A = 30°, a = 6, and b = 12. What is ∠B?
questions.explanation: sin B = 12 sin 30° / 6 = 1, so B = 90°. There is only one possible angle.

questions.question: ASA and AAS problems often require finding the third angle before applying the Law of Sines.
questions.explanation: Finding the third angle helps create the angle-side pair needed for the proportion.

questions.question: In △ABC, ∠B = 64°, ∠C = 51°, and b = 16. Find c to the nearest tenth.
In an SSA problem, why should you check 180° minus the angle found by inverse sine?
questions.correctAnswer: Because supplementary angles have the same sine value, so the supplement may create a second possible triangle if the angle sum is still less than 180°.
questions.explanation: The ambiguity comes from the sine of an acute angle matching the sine of its obtuse supplement.

questions.question: A student has ∠A = 55°, a = 15, and b = 20, then computes sin B ≈ 1.092. Explain the conclusion.
questions.correctAnswer: No triangle is possible because a sine value cannot be greater than 1, so the given measurements are inconsistent.
questions.explanation: A sine result greater than 1 is outside the possible range for real angles.
